verses.text: Now the Philistines gathered together their armies to battle; and they were gathered together at Socoh, which belongs to Judah, and encamped between Socoh and Azekah, in Ephesdammim.
Saul and the men of Israel were gathered together, and encamped in the valley of Elah, and set the battle in array against the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on the mountain on the one side, and Israel stood on the mountain on the other side: and there was a valley between them.
A champion out of the camp of the Philistines named Goliath, of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span  went out.
He had a helmet of brass on his head, and he wore a coat of mail; and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels  of brass.
He had brass shin armor on his legs, and a brass javelin between his shoulders.
The staff of his spear was like a weaver’s beam; and his spear’s head weighed six hundred shekels of iron.  His shield bearer went before him.

He stood and cried to the armies of Israel, and said to them, “Why have you come out to set your battle in array? Am I not a Philistine, and you servants to Saul? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me.
If he is able to fight with me and kill me, then will we be your servants; but if I prevail against him and kill him, then you will be our servants and serve us.”
The Philistine said, “I defy the armies of Israel today! Give me a man, that we may fight together!”
When Saul and all Israel heard those words of the Philistine, they were dismayed, and greatly afraid.
Now David was the son of that Ephrathite of Bethlehem Judah, whose name was Jesse; and he had eight sons. The man was an elderly old man in the days of Saul.
The three oldest sons of Jesse had gone after Saul to the battle: and the names of his three sons who went to the battle were Eliab the firstborn, and next to him Abinadab, and the third Shammah.
David was the youngest; and the three oldest followed Saul.
Now David went back and forth from Saul to feed his father’s sheep at Bethlehem.
The Philistine came near morning and evening, and presented himself forty days.
Jesse said to David his son, “Now take for your brothers an ephah  of this parched grain, and these ten loaves, and carry them quickly to the camp to your brothers;
and bring these ten cheeses to the captain of their thousand, and see how your brothers are doing, and bring back news.”
Now Saul, and they, and all the men of Israel, were in the valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines.

David rose up early in the morning, and left the sheep with a keeper, and took and went, as Jesse had commanded him. He came to the place of the wagons, as the army which was going out to the fight shouted for the battle.
Israel and the Philistines put the battle in array, army against army.
David left his baggage in the hand of the keeper of the baggage, and ran to the army, and came and greeted his brothers.
As he talked with them, behold, the champion, the Philistine of Gath, Goliath by name, came up out of the ranks of the Philistines, and said the same words; and David heard them.
All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him, and were terrified.

The men of Israel said, “Have you seen this man who has come up? He has surely come up to defy Israel. The king will give great riches to the man who kills him, and will give him his daughter, and make his father’s house free in Israel.”

David spoke to the men who stood by him, saying, “What shall be done to the man who kills this Philistine, and takes away the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?”
The people answered him in this way, saying, “So shall it be done to the man who kills him.”

Eliab his oldest brother heard when he spoke to the men; and Eliab’s anger burned against David, and he said, “Why have you come down? With whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride, and the naughtiness of your heart; for you have come down that you might see the battle.”
David said, “What have I now done? Is there not a cause?”
He turned away from him toward another, and spoke like that again; and the people answered him again the same way.
When the words were heard which David spoke, they rehearsed them before Saul; and he sent for him.
David said to Saul, “Let no man’s heart fail because of him. Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine.”
Saul said to David, “You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him; for you are but a youth, and he a man of war from his youth.”
David said to Saul, “Your servant was keeping his father’s sheep; and when a lion or a bear came, and took a lamb out of the flock,
I went out after him, and struck him, and rescued it out of his mouth. When he arose against me, I caught him by his beard, and struck him, and killed him.
Your servant struck both the lion and the bear. This uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, since he has defied the armies of the living God.”

David said, “Yahweh who delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine.” Saul said to David, “Go! Yahweh will be with you.”
Saul dressed David with his clothing. He put a helmet of brass on his head, and he clad him with a coat of mail.
David strapped his sword on his clothing, and he tried to move; for he had not tested it. David said to Saul, “I can’t go with these; for I have not tested them.” Then David took them off.

He took his staff in his hand, and chose for himself five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag which he had. His sling was in his hand; and he came near to the Philistine.
The Philistine walked and came near to David; and the man who bore the shield went before him.
When the Philistine looked around, and saw David, he disdained him; for he was but a youth, and ruddy, and had a good looking face.
The Philistine said to David, “Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?” The Philistine cursed David by his gods.
The Philistine said to David, “Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky, and to the animals of the field.”

Then David said to the Philistine, “You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of Yahweh of Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.

Today, Yahweh will deliver you into my hand. I will strike you, and take your head from off you. I will give the dead bodies of the army of the Philistines today to the birds of the sky, and to the wild animals of the earth; that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel,
and that all this assembly may know that Yahweh doesn’t save with sword and spear; for the battle is Yahweh’s, and he will give you into our hand.”
When the Philistine arose, and walked and came near to meet David, David hurried, and ran toward the army to meet the Philistine.
David put his hand in his bag, took a stone, and slung it, and struck the Philistine in his forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the earth.
So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck the Philistine, and killed him; but there was no sword in the hand of David.
Then David ran, stood over the Philistine, took his sword, drew it out of its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.

The men of Israel and of Judah arose and shouted, and pursued the Philistines as far as Gai and to the gates of Ekron. The wounded of the Philistines fell down by the way to Shaaraim, even to Gath and to Ekron.
The children of Israel returned from chasing after the Philistines and they plundered their camp.
David took the head of the Philistine, and brought it to Jerusalem; but he put his armor in his tent.
When Saul saw David go out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the captain of the army, “Abner, whose son is this youth?” Abner said, “As your soul lives, O king, I can’t tell.”
The king said, “Inquire whose son the young man is!”
As David returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him before Saul with the head of the Philistine in his hand.
Saul said to him, “Whose son are you, you young man?” David answered, “I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite.”

footnotes.content: The armies gather at Socoh and Azekah—places whose names we might forget, but the Lord remembers them as the stage where His faithfulness will show. We often think great things happen in famous cities, yet God's hand moves just as surely in quiet, ordinary places. There is no unholy ground when faith calls on the Almighty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul and Israel stood ready in the valley of Elah, arrayed for battle. How often do we stand with all our best preparations, yet trembling in our hearts? This moment teaches us that readiness of body is not the same as readiness of spirit. The Lord looks for trust first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A valley between two mountains—such a simple geography, yet it mirrors the spiritual landscape of every doubt we face. The chasm looks impossible to cross, and that is exactly where the Lord does His clearest work. We learn His faithfulness not on level ground, but when the valley shows us how small we are.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Goliath of Gath—a giant, towering, named and known. He stands for everything that seems to crush us: size, strength, reputation, the weight of fear. Yet a man with a name is still a man, and the Lord knows him as He knows all His creatures. Pride may stand very tall, but it stands on borrowed time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five thousand shekels of brass—such wealth spent on armor, such weight to bear. How much do we load ourselves with, thinking that more protection will bring more peace? The spirit carries lighter than any armor ever could, and the Lord's shield costs nothing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Brass shin armor, a javelin between his shoulders—every piece of him speaking power and invulnerability. How many of us have built such armor against hurt, only to find that beneath it we are just as afraid? True strength begins when we lay it down.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The spear's staff like a weaver's beam, the head weighing six hundred shekels—the specificity shows us how thoroughly the writer measured Goliath's power, yet by verse 50 all that weight will mean nothing. Sometimes the details of our trouble are just details; only our faith makes them matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Why have you come out to set your battle in array?" the giant mocks. He sees Israel as less than servants, not even worthy of a full battle. His contempt runs deep—and therein lies his first weakness. A man who despises his enemy has already begun to underestimate him, and the Lord often works through such blindness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "If he prevails against me...if I prevail against him." The terms sound fair, yet they hinge on a contest between the strong and the weak. We have all faced such lopsided odds in life—and how often have we learned that fairness is not the Lord's way of winning His battles? He prefers the impossible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Give me a man, that we may fight together!" The challenge comes not once but twice—his pride will not let it rest. How the enemy loves to make us hear his defiance again and again, as if repetition can wear down our faith. Yet each new day, the Lord's mercies are also new.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Saul and all Israel heard those words, they were dismayed and greatly afraid. Fear is honest; it is what we do with fear that matters. Israel's dismay showed them they could not win by their own strength—perhaps that was the truest gift the giant ever gave them, for it would teach them to look elsewhere.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now David—suddenly the story turns and we meet him. He is the son of Jesse, an Ephrathite, from the little town we all know by heart now. He is ordinary, even humble, yet he is the thread the Lord was weaving all along. How often do we look past the quiet one standing nearby, not knowing he is the answer to our prayer?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The three oldest sons of Jesse followed Saul to battle—they are where we think a man should be, doing what we think matters most. Yet it will be the one left behind with the sheep who remembers what truly matters. The Lord's ways delight in turning our sorting upside down.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David was the youngest; and the three oldest followed Saul. One sentence tells the whole story: he is overlooked, the afterthought, the least likely. The Lord speaks clearest through such humbling, for when He acts through the least, His hand alone can be seen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David went back and forth from Saul to feed his father's sheep at Bethlehem—a keeper of sheep, the gentlest of callings. How many prayers rise from a shepherd's watch? How many prayers does a man pray alone with God and the flock? The Lord was fashioning David in those quiet hours, preparing him not to be noticed, but to be faithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Philistine came near morning and evening and presented himself forty days. Forty—the number of testing, of wandering in the wilderness until readiness comes. For forty days Israel listened to their fear grow louder. For forty days the Lord was preparing a boy in the fields to hear it and say no.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jesse sends David to bring bread and cheese to his brothers—an errand, a simple father's task. How tender this is: the Lord does not summon David with thunder; He uses the quiet voice of a father's love. We are often at our post not because we chose glory, but because someone we love asked us to serve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "See how your brothers are doing, and bring back news." A messenger on an errand—how modest, how unremarkable. Yet the Lord sends us where we are needed exactly when we are needed, and we often do not know it until we arrive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul and all the men of Israel were in the valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines. The armies are locked in stalemate, afraid to break rank. Stalemate is not peace—it is paralysis dressed as caution. How many of us live there, afraid to move, thinking stillness is safety?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David rose up early in the morning, left the sheep with a keeper, and went as his father commanded. There is no reluctance here, no delay. Obedience is the quickest path to where the Lord means you to be—and David moves toward his destiny with the simplicity of a boy obeying his father. How far such obedience reaches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel and the Philistines put the battle in array, army against army. They are ready for a war of noise and weight and numbers. Neither army knows that the battle will be decided by a stone, and everything they arranged will become beside the point. How often do we prepare for the wrong kind of battle?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David left his baggage and ran to greet his brothers—nothing weighing him down, nothing held back. A young man arriving with bread and hope, unarmored and clear-eyed. How the Lord uses the unencumbered heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As David talked with his brothers, Goliath came up out of the ranks and said the same words—and David heard them. In that moment, history turns. David does not run from the sound; he hears it and something in him answers. When we listen aright, we hear not terror but a call to trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were terrified. Fear is contagious—it spreads like a cold through an army. Yet in that very crowd, one boy hears the same giant and feels something altogether different. What we see in a trial depends entirely on what eye we look with.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The king will give great riches to the man who kills him, and will give him his daughter, and make his father's house free in Israel." Tempting rewards, and yet David asks a different question next—not what he will gain, but what honor the Lord will receive. That difference marks the whole chapter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "What shall be done to the man who kills this Philistine, and takes away the reproach from Israel?" David's question looks outward to the shame on God's name, inward to what faith asks of him. He does not ask about reward; he asks about remedy. This is the prayer of a soul already decided.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people answered him in the same way, telling him the rewards Saul had named. They see a young man asking questions and assume he is calculating advantage. We often mistake eagerness for greed, not knowing the heart behind the asking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eliab's anger burned against David—his own brother turns on him with contempt. "Why have you come down? I know your pride and your naughtiness." How it stings to be misread by those closest to us, yet David does not defend himself. A clear conscience can bear such words and move on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Is there not a cause?" David's answer is brief, almost breathless with urgency. He does not argue with his brother or prove his heart. He simply restates the matter: there is a cause, and it matters more than any quarrel between them. Single-heartedness silences many objections.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He turned away and spoke like that again to another man; and the people answered him the same way again. David keeps asking, each time receiving the same answer about riches and rank. His persistence shows he is not trying to win the argument—he is trying to understand what needs to be said and done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When his words were heard, they rehearsed them before Saul, and Saul sent for him. The king's men bring David before Saul—not because David pushed himself forward, but because his words had already traveled ahead, carrying something the king's tired heart could recognize. Faithfulness announces itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Let no man's heart fail because of him. Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine." David speaks to Saul as a servant, yet his certainty is absolute. There is no boasting here, only the simple statement of a man who has already settled his course in his heart. Such calm comes from prayer, not from strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him; for you are but a youth, and he a man of war from his youth." Saul sees youth and inexperience. He does not yet see what David knows of himself—not from pride, but from watching the Lord deliver him again and again in the pasture. Age and strength are not the only teachers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Your servant was keeping his father's sheep; and when a lion or a bear came and took a lamb out of the flock..." Here David speaks of the pasture—that humble, hidden place. A shepherd facing down a lion or a bear, alone in the fields with nothing but his staff and his love for the flock. Every trial we endure in secret becomes strength for the trial that comes in public.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I went out after him, and struck him, and rescued the lamb out of his mouth." David describes his own courage without shame, yet without pride. He speaks of what he did because it is the truth, and the truth matters more than modesty. Sometimes we must name what the Lord has done through us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Your servant struck both the lion and the bear. This uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, since he has defied the armies of the living God." David draws the line clearly: the Philistine's boast is not against Israel alone, but against the Lord Himself. That changes everything—it is no longer a matter of military might, but of God's honor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Yahweh who delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine." Faith speaks in such simple logic: if the Lord has kept me through smaller trials, He will keep me through greater ones. Saul hears this and says, "Go! Yahweh will be with you."—for what else can a king say when confronted with such certainty?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul dressed David with his own clothing, a helmet of brass, a coat of mail. The king gives what a king has to give—the protection of a king's armor. Yet armor means nothing without the faith to wear it, and David's faith is not in brass or iron.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David strapped on Saul's sword and tried to move; for he had not tested it. "I can't go with these," David said, "for I have not tested them." Then he took them off. How honest this is—David knows what works and what does not, what is familiar and what is strange. He does not accept a gift that will weigh him down.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He took his staff in his hand and chose for himself five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in the pouch of his shepherd's bag. His sling was in his hand; and he came near to the Philistine. What poetry in this simplicity—stones from a brook, a shepherd's pouch, a sling. The weapons of a boy, yet they will accomplish what all Saul's armor could not. The Lord delights in such reversals.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Philistine walked and came near to David; and the man who bore his shield went before him. Even now, Goliath comes with armor-bearer and weight and ritual. He moves as power always moves—loudly, heavily, announced. David will come as grace comes—simply, suddenly, undeniable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the Philistine looked around and saw David, he disdained him; for he was but a youth, ruddy, and with a good looking face. Goliath measures David and judges him by the eyes of the flesh—youth, appearance, obvious weakness. He sees exactly what David is and despises him for it. His contempt is his blindness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?" Goliath mocks the shepherd's staff and sling, calling them nothing. Yet the staff has shepherded a thousand moments, and the sling has turned back wild beasts. What the mighty dismiss, the faithful have long proven true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and to the animals of the field." Goliath speaks his threat as the final word, as if he has already won. How the enemy loves to announce his victory before the battle is joined, trying to steal our will before the first blow. Yet the battle belongs to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of Yahweh of Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied." David speaks, and in his words, the whole truth is laid bare: he comes not in his own strength but in the name of the Most High God. This is the moment—not when the stone flies, but when the prayer is voiced.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Today, Yahweh will deliver you into my hand. I will strike you, and take your head from off you. I will give the dead bodies of the army of the Philistines today to the birds of the sky...that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel." David speaks with the certainty of one who has already seen it in his spirit. He is not predicting; he is announcing what the Lord has already decided. Such faith speaks in the past tense before the future unfolds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "And that all this assembly may know that Yahweh doesn't save with sword and spear; for the battle is Yahweh's, and he will give you into our hand." The core truth stands revealed: the battle does not belong to Israel's strength, nor to their armor, nor to their numbers. It belongs to the Lord alone. Everything else is just the stage He chooses for His glory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the Philistine arose and walked and came near to meet David, David hurried and ran toward the army to meet the Philistine. David does not wait; he does not hesitate; he does not retreat. He runs forward with the eagerness of a man already at peace. The battle is the Lord's—he has only to show up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David put his hand in his bag, took a stone, and slung it, and struck the Philistine in his forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the earth. One stone from a boy's pouch, and Goliath falls. One moment of faithful action, and everything is undone. This is how the Lord works—through the smallest obedience, the greatest victories.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck the Philistine, and killed him; but there was no sword in the hand of David. The weapons of his youth, the simplest tools—these were enough. All Saul's armor lay behind him, unused. When we lean on the Lord, we need carry nothing else.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David ran and stood over the Philistine, took his sword, drew it out of its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled. The enemy's own weapon becomes the instrument of his defeat. How often the Lord turns what was meant to destroy us into the very thing that saves us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The men of Israel and of Judah arose and shouted, and pursued the Philistines as far as Gai and to the gates of Ekron. Suddenly the paralyzed army moves—freed not by their own strength, but by the death of the one thing they feared. How much of our paralysis is born only of unchallenged fear?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The children of Israel returned from chasing after the Philistines and they plundered their camp. Victory brings its own rewards—yet David did not fight for spoils. He fought for the honor of God, and the rest followed. Always, when we seek the Lord first, the other gifts settle into place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem; but he put his armor in his tent. The trophy goes to the capital; the armor is kept. David does not vanish into pride or excess. He takes what is his due and holds it simply, as a shepherd would.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Saul saw David go out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, "Abner, whose son is this youth?" Abner said, "I can't tell." The king does not recognize the boy he only just armed. How fitting—Saul had looked at David through the eyes of duty and obligation. Now, having seen him move in faith, Saul asks who he truly is, not knowing the answer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king said, "Inquire whose son the young man is!" Saul's curiosity has turned urgent. Something in David's victory has spoken to the king's heart—not the courage, but the source of the courage. Saul is searching for understanding he does not yet have.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As David returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, Abner took him and brought him before Saul with the head of the Philistine in his hand. David stands before the king, not asking for recognition or reward, but simply presenting what he has done. The trophy in his hand speaks louder than any boast.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Saul said to him, "Whose son are you, you young man?" David answered, "I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite." The circle closes—David names himself without flourish, without claiming more than he is. He is the son of Jesse, a servant's son. Yet in that hour, he had shown a king what it means to trust the Lord with all your heart. The question Saul asked is answered, but not in the way Saul expected.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
